rows.request: also how deep is the everything as file theology in Linux v3.0.1, because I would just like the processes to be in proper virtual heap/stack with a proper memory address and not some /proc/bullshit
rows.final_reply:
That's the real picture. Here's the breakdown:

---

## The Layers

### Layer 1 — Pure kernel structs (no files, ever)

| Struct | File | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `task_struct` | `include/linux/sched.h` | Every process/thread — PID, state, priority, signals |
| `mm_struct` | `include/linux/mm_types.h:220` | The entire virtual address space of a process |
| `vm_area_struct` | `include/linux/mm_types.h:132` | Each individual segment — stack, heap, code, mmap regions |

These live in kernel memory. You touch them **only through syscalls** — `fork`, `execve`, `mmap`, `brk`, `kill`, `wait`. No file path involved. This is where your "proper virtual heap/stack with memory addresses" actually lives.

### Layer 2 — `/proc` (completely optional, mount it or don't)

`/proc` is a **virtual filesystem** that just reflects those kernel structs back as readable files for userspace tools like `ps` and `top`. It is:

- Not mounted unless you call `mount("proc", "/proc", "procfs", ...)`
- **Not required** for process management — `kill(pid, sig)` works fine without it
- Compiled out with `CONFIG_PROC_FS=n` if you don't want it at all

### Layer 3 — `/sys` (also optional, hardware/driver info)

Same story — reflects kernel driver data structures. `CONFIG_SYSFS=n` removes it.

### Layer 4 — `/dev` (required for I/O, not for process management)

You need this for terminals, storage, etc. but it has nothing to do with how processes are scheduled or managed in memory.

---

## So for minit — you need zero /proc

Your process manager works entirely through syscalls:

```c
fork()          // kernel creates a new task_struct, clones mm_struct
execve()        // kernel replaces mm_struct segments with new program
waitpid(pid)    // kernel checks task_struct exit state
kill(pid, sig)  // kernel sets signal in task_struct
kill(-1, SIGKILL) // kernel iterates all task_structs, sends signal
```

The kernel is doing all the `task_struct` / `mm_struct` / `vm_area_struct` bookkeeping internally. `/proc` is just a window into that — you can ignore it entirely.

---

## If You Want Zero "Everything is a File"

```
CONFIG_PROC_FS=n       # no /proc
CONFIG_SYSFS=n         # no /sys
CONFIG_DEVTMPFS=n      # no auto /dev (you manage devices manually)
```

What you're left with is the kernel as a pure **syscall interface** to hardware + scheduler + memory manager. Processes exist as kernel structs with real virtual address spaces. No filesystem metaphor involved. That's actually the clean Unix model before the `/proc` layer got bolted on.

rows.request: perfect so we are removing /proc because thats one half of people screwing up their system, because /proc allows people to accidentally kill even the basic system processes
rows.final_reply:
Good. Here's the full picture of what removing `/proc` actually cuts off and what else you should kill alongside it:

---

## What to Disable in `.config`

```
CONFIG_PROC_FS=n          # kills /proc entirely
CONFIG_PROC_KCORE=n       # /proc/kcore — exposes RAW KERNEL MEMORY, huge hole
CONFIG_PROC_SYSCTL=n      # /proc/sys — runtime kernel parameter changes
CONFIG_PROC_PAGE_MONITOR=n
CONFIG_MAGIC_SYSRQ=n      # /proc/sysrq-trigger — can halt/kill/unmount anything
CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC=n    # /proc/config.gz
```

`CONFIG_MAGIC_SYSRQ` especially — that's the other half of the problem. Even without `/proc`, SysRq key combos on the keyboard can `kill -9` everything or force-unmount filesystems. Kill it.

---

## What Breaks (That You Don't Care About)

These kernel features have `depends on PROC_FS` so they auto-disable — all fine for your setup:

| Feature | Why you don't need it |
|---|---|
| `SLABINFO` | Memory allocator debug info — dev tool |
| `NET_DCCPPROBE` | Network debugging probe |
| `PROC_SYSCTL` | Runtime kernel tuning — you set config at build time |
| `IKCONFIG_PROC` | Reading kernel config at runtime — irrelevant |
| `SCTP`/`WIRELESS` proc entries | Network subsystem stats |

---

## What This Actually Means for Security

Without `/proc`, the **only** way to interact with a process is:

1. You already have its PID (your minit handed it to you via the socket API)
2. You have the right `uid`/`gid` to send it a signal
3. You go through minit's socket which applies your rules

Nobody can enumerate running processes. Nobody can `kill -9 1`. Nobody can poke `/proc/kcore` and read kernel memory. The attack surface collapses to just the syscall interface — and syscalls require you to already know what you're targeting.

---

## One Thing to Keep in Mind

Without `/proc`, you also lose `/proc/mounts`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/cpuinfo` etc. — which is fine since you have no `ps`, `top`, or `free` anyway. But if you ever want **minit itself** to report system stats through its socket API (memory free, CPU load), you'd query the kernel directly via:

- `sysinfo()` syscall — memory, load average, uptime
- `getrusage()` — per-process resource usage
- `clock_gettime()` — timing

No `/proc` needed. Minit can expose all of that through its own socket in whatever format you want, keeping everything under your control.
